subject: freediving depth
title: What If You Dove 100 Meters on One Breath?

scenes.text: What if you dove 100 meters on one breath? Sinking is easy. Coming back up is the problem.
At 10 meters, the pressure doubles. Your heart slows, sometimes to just 20 to 30 beats a minute.
By about 20 meters you stop floating. From there, you sink without kicking, in a silent free fall.
At 100 meters, your lungs are squeezed to about one eleventh of their size. Blood shifts into your chest.
The deepest single breath dive ever, in 2007, reached 214 meters. Few humans have gone past 100.
Then the ascent. As pressure drops, so does the oxygen in your lungs. Blackouts usually strike in the top three meters, almost home.

description:
What if you dove 100 meters on one breath? Pressure doubles by 10 meters, the dive reflex can slow the heart to 20-30 beats a minute, divers free-fall below about 20 meters, and at 100 meters the lungs shrink to about one eleventh of their surface volume.
On the way up, falling pressure lowers oxygen in the lungs, which is why blackouts usually happen near the surface.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: How long can you hold your breath? Don't test it in water. Tell us the extreme body what-if we should run through next.
